fact: People of Internet calls Law No. 175 of 2018 on Anti-Cyber and Information Technology Crimes Egypt's principal cybercrime statute.

People of Internet says Egyptian courts convicted a series of TikTok content creators under Article 25 of Law 175/2018 in November 2025, with sentences from six-month suspended terms to two years and a fine of EGP 100,000 each.
The Senate legislative committee is reviewing two impact studies on the effectiveness of Law 175 of 2018 on combating information technology crimes, as an existing law.

fact: Assistant interior minister Ashraf Abdel Aziz says Law 175 of 2018 on information technology crimes covers most digital crimes and will serve for years, while Senator Mahmoud Salah Saad proposes raising maximum penalties under arts. 25 and 26.

fact: LDSF describes Anti-Cybercrime Law No. 175 of 2018, including Article 25 on family values, as the law under which authorities prosecute content creators.

LDSF reports the Cairo Economic Court on 29 November 2025 sentenced video blogger Mohamed Abdel Aaty to two years and a fine under the Anti-Cybercrime Law, and sentenced Qamar El-Wekala to six months.
The Economic Court's reasoning applies Law 175 of 2018 on combating information technology crimes and its executive regulations (PM Decree 1699 of 2020).
The Economic Court tried a blogger on a charge under article 27 of Law 175 of 2018 (running a site to commit a crime) and acquitted her on it, while sentencing her on two other counts.
Youm7 names the cybercrime law, Law 175 of 2018, as Egypt's legal framework against cybercrime and its penalties.
Youm7 reports that a Public Prosecution course held on 8-12 November 2026 teaches the provisions of Egypt's Law 175 of 2018 on information technology crimes, including search and seizure warrants.
CPJ says Article 7 of Egypt's Anti-Cybercrime Law lets the investigating authority order a website blocked.
The Egyptian Human Rights Forum report describes Article 7 of the Anti-Cybercrime Law as letting the investigative authority order a website blocked, to be put to a court within 24 hours.
